title: Testing Strategy: Mocks & Integration
summary: A good Go testing strategy is a **pyramid**: many fast unit tests that fake dependencies through small interfaces, a smaller layer of **integration tests** that exercise real collaborators (a database, a queue), and a few end-to-end tests. Go's `testing` package, table-driven tests, interface-based fakes, and build tags are the tools that make this practical.

subtopics.title: The test pyramid
subtopics.explanation: Most tests should be fast unit tests with no I/O. A thinner middle layer of integration tests checks that your code talks to real dependencies (DB, HTTP, broker) correctly. A few end-to-end tests verify the whole system. The wider the layer, the cheaper and faster each test must be.
subtopics.example:
go test ./...      // unit tests, milliseconds
go test -tags=integration ./...  // slower, real deps

subtopics.title: Interfaces as test seams
subtopics.explanation: You can only fake what you depend on through an interface. Define small consumer-side interfaces (e.g. a UserStore with the two methods you actually call) and inject them. In tests you pass a fake; in production you pass the real implementation. This is the single most important enabler of testable Go.
subtopics.example: type UserStore interface { Get(id string) (User, error) }

subtopics.title: Fakes vs mocks vs stubs
subtopics.explanation: A stub returns canned values. A fake is a working but simplified implementation (e.g. an in-memory map standing in for a database). A mock additionally records and asserts on the calls it received. Prefer hand-written fakes for state and lightweight mocks only when verifying interactions matters.
subtopics.example: type fakeStore struct{ m map[string]User } // a fake, not a mock

subtopics.title: Table-driven tests & subtests
subtopics.explanation: Idiomatic Go expresses many cases as a slice of structs and loops over them, running each as a named subtest with t.Run. Subtests give you isolated failures, parallelism with t.Parallel(), and the ability to run one case with -run.
subtopics.example: for _, tc := range cases { t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T){ ... }) }

subtopics.title: Separating integration tests with build tags
subtopics.explanation: Integration tests need real infrastructure and are slow, so gate them behind a build tag (//go:build integration) or skip with testing.Short(). The default `go test ./...` stays fast; CI runs the slow suite explicitly with -tags=integration.

subtopics.title: httptest and testcontainers
subtopics.explanation: net/http/httptest spins up a real in-process server so you can test HTTP clients and handlers without the network. For databases and brokers, the testcontainers-go library starts a real Postgres/Redis in Docker for the duration of the test, giving high-fidelity integration coverage.

foundations.overview: Testing in Go is deliberately minimal: one `testing` package, the `go test` command, and a strong cultural convention of table-driven tests. The hard part is not the syntax — it is strategy. Which dependencies do you fake, which do you exercise for real, and how do you keep the fast tests fast while still proving the system works end to end? The answer is to design code around small interfaces so you can swap real collaborators for fakes, and to separate the slow integration suite from the quick unit suite.
foundations.formalDefinition: A Go test is a function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in a `_test.go` file, discovered and run by `go test`. A testing strategy is the deliberate allocation of coverage across unit tests (isolated, fast, dependencies faked through interfaces) and integration tests (real collaborators, slower, often gated by build tags).
foundations.whyItMatters: Tests are the safety net that lets a team refactor and ship daily. A strategy that over-mocks gives green tests that prove nothing about production; one that integrates everything is too slow to run on every save. Getting the balance right is what separates a maintainable Go codebase from a fragile one, and it is a frequent senior-interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a pyramid. The wide base is unit tests — cheap, numerous, run on every keystroke. The middle is integration tests against real dependencies — fewer, slower, run in CI. The narrow tip is end-to-end tests — a handful, run before release. Interfaces are the doors you open to swap a real dependency for a fake at the unit layer.
foundations.runtimePerspective: `go test` compiles the package together with its `_test.go` files into a temporary test binary and runs it. Files tagged `//go:build integration` are simply excluded from the build unless you pass `-tags=integration`, so the compiler never even sees them in the fast path. `testing.Short()` is just a flag (`-short`) you read at runtime to skip slow cases.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every serious Go service has table-driven unit tests for business logic, httptest for handlers and clients, an in-memory fake for the database in unit tests, and a testcontainers-backed integration suite that runs against a real Postgres in CI before merge.
foundations.businessImpact: A fast, trustworthy test suite shortens the feedback loop, lets teams deploy multiple times a day, and catches regressions before customers do — directly reducing incident cost and increasing release velocity.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Designing for testability (small interfaces, dependency injection) also produces loosely coupled, easier-to-change code. The discipline of writing tests forces clearer module boundaries.
foundations.performanceImpact: Unit tests with faked I/O run in milliseconds, so developers actually run them. Integration tests are orders of magnitude slower (Docker startup, real queries), which is exactly why they are gated and run less often; mixing them into the fast path destroys the feedback loop.
commonUseCases: Table-driven unit tests for pure business logic
Hand-written in-memory fakes injected through interfaces
httptest servers/recorders for HTTP clients and handlers
Build-tag-gated integration tests against real Postgres/Redis via testcontainers

commonMisconceptions.reality: Over-mocking tests your mocks, not your code. Tests that assert 'method X was called' often pass even when the integration is broken; prefer state-based fakes and real integration tests at the boundaries.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need a mocking framework to test Go.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go's interfaces make hand-written fakes trivial. Frameworks like gomock help for large interfaces, but a 10-line struct is usually clearer and has no codegen step.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Integration tests should run on every save.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are slow by design. Gate them behind a build tag or -short so the fast unit suite stays sub-second; run the slow suite in CI.

visualExplorer.title: From real dependency to fake: the seam
visualExplorer.caption: How an interface lets you inject a fake in tests and the real implementation in production.

config.intro: Turning a hard-to-test dependency into a swappable seam:

steps.name: Identify the dependency
steps.detail: Your service needs a database. Calling *sql.DB directly makes the service untestable without a real DB.

steps.name: Define a consumer-side interface
steps.detail: Declare a small interface with only the methods you use: type UserStore interface { Get(id string) (User, error) }.

steps.name: Depend on the interface
steps.detail: The service struct holds a UserStore, not a concrete *sql.DB. This is the seam.

steps.name: Inject the real impl in main
steps.detail: Production wires a *PostgresStore (which satisfies UserStore) into the service.

steps.name: Inject a fake in tests
steps.detail: Unit tests pass a fakeStore backed by a map — no database, runs in microseconds.

visualExplorer.title: Anatomy of a table-driven test
visualExplorer.caption: How `go test` runs each row of a table as an isolated subtest.

config.intro: What happens when you run a table-driven test:

steps.name: Define cases
steps.detail: A slice of structs, each with a name, inputs, and expected output.

steps.name: Range over cases
steps.detail: Loop over the slice; each iteration is one logical test.

steps.name: t.Run a subtest
steps.detail: t.Run(tc.name, ...) runs each case as a named subtest, so failures point at a specific row.

steps.name: Optional t.Parallel()
steps.detail: Marking subtests parallel runs independent cases concurrently, speeding up large tables.

steps.name: Targeted reruns
steps.detail: go test -run TestX/specific_case reruns just the failing row.

interactiveExamples.title: Inject a fake through an interface
interactiveExamples.explanation: The Greeter depends on a UserStore interface, not a concrete database. The test passes an in-memory fake, so it runs with no I/O. This is the core pattern that makes Go code testable.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: convert to a table-driven test
interactiveExamples.explanation: The starter tests one case with copy-pasted asserts. Rewrite it as a table-driven test with named subtests so each case fails independently and you can target one with -run.

checkpoints.prompt: You want a fast unit test for a service that normally writes to Postgres. What is the idiomatic Go approach?
options: Spin up a real Postgres in every unit test
Define a small interface for the DB operations the service uses and inject an in-memory fake in the test
Comment out the database calls before running tests
Use a global mock variable that every test mutates
checkpoints.explanation: Depending on a small consumer-side interface lets you inject an in-memory fake in unit tests (fast, no I/O) and the real *sql.DB-backed implementation in production. Spinning up real Postgres belongs in a gated integration test, not the fast unit path.

checkpoints.prompt: A test file begins with this build constraint. What does plain `go test ./...` do with it?
options: Runs the file's tests as usual
Skips compiling the file entirely (tests not run)
Runs the tests but marks them as skipped in output
checkpoints.explanation: The //go:build integration constraint excludes the file from the build unless you pass -tags=integration. Without the tag the compiler never includes it, so its tests simply don't exist in the fast suite — no skip message, no run.

checkpoints.prompt: This 'mock-heavy' test passes even when the real save logic is broken. Why is that a problem?
options: It only asserts that Save was called, not that the user was persisted correctly — it tests the mock, not real behavior
saver should be an interface not a struct
User must be passed by pointer
checkpoints.explanation: Interaction-only assertions ('Save was called') pass regardless of whether the data was correct or whether the real store would accept it. Prefer a stateful fake (assert the stored value) plus an integration test against a real DB to prove persistence actually works.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so this slow test is skipped when the developer runs `go test -short`.
options: if testing.Short() { t.Skip("skipping integration test in short mode") }
checkpoints.explanation: testing.Short() reports whether -short was passed. Calling t.Skip when it's true lets developers run a fast subset locally while CI runs the full suite without -short.

codeLab.title: Test a service with a hand-written fake
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Register(store UserStore, name string) (string, error)` that rejects an empty name with an error, otherwise stores the user via `store.Save` and returns the generated id `"u:" + name`. The provided test harness uses an in-memory fake — make it pass.
hints: Validate the empty-name case first and return ErrEmptyName so errors.Is can match it.
Build the id deterministically ("u:" + name) so the test can assert an exact value.
Wrap the store error with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) so callers keep the original error in the chain.

debuggingLab.title: Flaky HTTP client test and leaked server
debuggingLab.symptom: A test for an HTTP client sometimes hangs or leaks goroutines, and `go test -race` occasionally complains about a connection used after the test ends.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two problems. First, the httptest server is never closed, so it (and its listener/goroutines) leaks for the rest of the test binary's life. Second, Fetch uses a client with no timeout, so if the handler ever blocks the test can hang forever. Tests must clean up their servers and bound their I/O.
commonMistakes: Forgetting defer srv.Close() on an httptest server.
Using http.DefaultClient (no timeout) inside code under test.
Ignoring the error from Fetch, hiding real failures.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Close the server with defer, give the client a timeout, and check the returned error.

theory.question: What is the difference between a stub, a fake, and a mock, and which should you prefer in Go?
theory.directAnswer: A stub returns hard-coded values. A fake is a real but simplified implementation, like an in-memory map standing in for a database. A mock additionally records calls and lets you assert on the interactions. In Go, prefer hand-written stateful fakes for most unit tests because they verify behavior (what was stored) rather than implementation details (what was called); reach for mocks only when the interaction itself is the contract.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three flavors of test double that stand in for a real dependency behind an interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real dependencies (DBs, networks) are slow and non-deterministic; doubles let unit tests run fast and reliably.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You define a small interface, then in tests pass a struct that satisfies it — returning canned values (stub), maintaining state (fake), or recording and asserting calls (mock).

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right double determines whether your tests catch real bugs or just lock in the current implementation, a key senior-level judgment.
theory.realWorldExample: An in-memory fakeUserStore backed by a map lets you test order logic without a database, asserting the stored order rather than that Save was called.

followUps.question: When is over-mocking harmful?
followUps.answer: When tests assert call sequences instead of outcomes, they pass even when the integration is broken and break on harmless refactors — high maintenance, low value.

followUps.question: Do you need gomock or testify in Go?
followUps.answer: Not usually. Interfaces make hand-written fakes trivial; frameworks help only for large interfaces or when generated mocks reduce boilerplate.

theory.question: How do you keep a fast unit-test suite while still running real integration tests?
theory.directAnswer: Separate the two suites. Keep unit tests dependency-free so `go test ./...` runs in well under a second. Gate integration tests behind a build tag like //go:build integration (or skip them when testing.Short() is true), and run them explicitly in CI with `go test -tags=integration ./...`, often against real services started by testcontainers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A two-tier split: fast, isolated unit tests and slower, real-dependency integration tests.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Developers will only run a suite that is fast; integration tests are inherently slow, so they must not pollute the fast path.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Build tags exclude integration files from the default build; CI opts in with -tags. testcontainers-go starts real Postgres/Redis in Docker for the integration run.

theory.whyImportant: Mixing slow and fast tests destroys the feedback loop and is a common cause of teams abandoning their test suite.
theory.realWorldExample: Local development runs `go test -short ./...` in 200ms; the CI pipeline adds a job that runs `go test -tags=integration ./...` against a Dockerized Postgres.

followUps.question: What does testing.Short() do?
followUps.answer: It returns true when -short is passed, letting tests call t.Skip to opt out of slow work without removing the test.

followUps.question: Why use testcontainers over a shared test DB?
followUps.answer: Each test run gets an isolated, ephemeral container, avoiding cross-test contamination and 'works on my machine' drift from a long-lived shared database.

scenario.question: Your team's test suite is 95% green, takes 12 minutes, and yet a serializer bug shipped to production. What's likely wrong with the strategy and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The suite is probably mock-heavy: it asserts that methods were called rather than exercising the real serializer and storage paths, so a bug in actual encoding slips through. The 12-minute runtime suggests slow tests are mixed into the default path. Fix it by adding integration tests that round-trip through the real serializer and a real (testcontainer) datastore, replacing brittle interaction mocks with stateful fakes, and splitting the slow suite behind a build tag so unit tests stay fast.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A coverage-shaped-like-an-hourglass anti-pattern: many mocks, few real integrations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Over-mocking is easy to write and always green, giving false confidence.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interaction assertions don't execute the real encode/decode or DB path, so defects there are invisible to the suite.

scenario.whyImportant: Green suites that don't catch real bugs erode trust and are a classic senior debugging scenario.
scenario.realWorldExample: A JSON field tag typo serialized 'usr_id' instead of 'user_id'; only an integration test that decoded the real payload would have caught it.

followUps.question: How would you decide what to integration-test?
followUps.answer: Test the seams that touch the outside world — serialization, DB queries, HTTP contracts — for real, and unit-test pure logic in isolation.

coding.question: Write a table-driven test for `func ParseRange(s string) (lo, hi int, err error)` that parses strings like "3-7". Cover valid, reversed, and malformed input.
coding.thoughtProcess: Enumerate the behaviors: a valid range returns lo/hi; a reversed range ("7-3") should error; malformed input ("abc", "1-") should error. Express each as a row in a table with a name, input, expected values, and a wantErr flag, then run each as a subtest so failures are isolated.
coding.lineByLine: The cases slice lists every behavior with a descriptive name and a wantErr flag. The loop runs each case as a named subtest via t.Run, so a failure names the exact row. On the error path we assert err != nil and return early so we don't compare meaningless lo/hi values; on the success path we assert both bounds. This single test covers the whole contract and is trivial to extend by adding rows.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the number of cases — each runs once.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) per case beyond the static table.

followUps.question: Why run cases as subtests instead of a flat loop?
followUps.answer: Subtests give named, isolated failures, allow -run to target one case, and can opt into t.Parallel() independently.

followUps.question: How would you also fuzz ParseRange?
followUps.answer: Add a FuzzParseRange that feeds random strings and asserts it never panics and that any returned range satisfies lo <= hi.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Design for testability: depend on small, consumer-side interfaces and inject dependencies (constructor injection) so production wires real implementations and tests wire fakes. Keep pure business logic free of I/O so the bulk of your tests need no doubles at all.
productionDeepDive.performance: Keep the default `go test ./...` sub-second by faking I/O; gate slow integration tests behind build tags. Use t.Parallel() on independent subtests and cache test dependencies in CI. Profile slow tests — a single un-gated container start can dominate the suite.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Always run CI with `go test -race`. Make fakes safe for concurrent use if the code under test calls them from multiple goroutines, and prefer deterministic, order-independent assertions for concurrent code paths.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Treat flaky tests as bugs, not noise: remove time.Sleep-based synchronization, close httptest servers with defer, and give every test bounded timeouts. Reset shared state (and isolated containers) between integration tests.
productionDeepDive.observability: Track suite runtime and flakiness rates in CI; use `go test -json` piped to a test-reporting tool. Coverage (`go test -cover`) is a guide, not a target — high coverage with interaction mocks can still miss real bugs.
productionDeepDive.security: Never embed real credentials in test fixtures; load secrets from the environment and use throwaway testcontainer credentials. Scrub PII from golden files and test logs.

caseStudies.problem: Test HTTP clients and handlers without real network sockets.
caseStudies.solution: net/http/httptest provides an in-process server and a ResponseRecorder.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly higher fidelity than pure mocks at near-zero cost; still not a real TCP/TLS path.
caseStudies.lessons: An in-process real server beats a hand-rolled HTTP mock for confidence and clarity.

caseStudies.problem: Integration tests drifted from production because they used SQLite mocks of Postgres.
caseStudies.solution: Run a real ephemeral Postgres in Docker per test run via testcontainers.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slower and requires Docker, so it is gated behind a build tag in CI only.
caseStudies.lessons: High-fidelity integration tests against the real engine catch SQL and migration bugs that mocks hide.

keyTakeaways: Shape your tests like a pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a handful of end-to-end tests.
Small consumer-side interfaces are the seam that lets you inject hand-written fakes in unit tests and real implementations in production.
Prefer stateful fakes that assert outcomes over mocks that assert call sequences — over-mocking tests your mocks, not your code.
Gate slow integration tests behind //go:build integration or testing.Short(), run them in CI (often via testcontainers), and always use go test -race.
